blocks.text: How can we fairly compare two algorithms and predict outcomes based on data?

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore how to design experiments to compare algorithms and use linear regression to model relationships between variables. We will also discuss why correlation does not imply causation.

blocks.title: Experiment
blocks.text: An experiment is a procedure carried out to support, refute, or validate a hypothesis. It involves manipulating one or more variables to determine their effect on other variables.

blocks.markdown: When comparing two algorithms, it's crucial to ensure that the comparison is fair. This means controlling for variables that could influence the results, such as hardware, input data, and execution environment.

blocks.title: Fair Comparison
blocks.text: A fair comparison of algorithms requires consistent conditions, repeatable tests, and unbiased measurement of performance metrics.

blocks.title: Designing a Fair Experiment
blocks.prompt: How would you set up an experiment to compare the performance of two sorting algorithms?

steps.text: Identify the performance metric, such as execution time or memory usage.
Ensure both algorithms run on the same hardware and software environment.
Use the same set of input data for both algorithms to ensure consistency.
Repeat the experiment multiple times to account for variability and take the average result.

blocks.answer: By controlling these factors, you can ensure that the comparison between the two sorting algorithms is fair and unbiased.

blocks.markdown: Next, we will explore linear regression, a statistical method used to model the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables.

blocks.title: Linear Regression
blocks.text: Linear regression is a method for modeling the relationship between a scalar response (dependent variable) and one or more explanatory variables (independent variables).

blocks.caption: The equation for simple linear regression, where \( y \) is the dependent variable, \( x \) is the independent variable, \( \beta_0 \) is the intercept, \( \beta_1 \) is the slope, and \( \epsilon \) is the error term.

blocks.title: Fitting a Simple Linear Regression
blocks.prompt: Given a dataset of heights and weights, how would you fit a simple linear regression model?

steps.text: Identify the dependent variable (weight) and the independent variable (height).
Use statistical software or methods to calculate the best-fit line, determining \( \beta_0 \) and \( \beta_1 \).
Interpret the slope \( \beta_1 \) as the expected change in weight for a one-unit increase in height.

blocks.answer: By fitting the model, you can predict weight based on height and understand the relationship between the two variables.

blocks.markdown: While linear regression can show a relationship between variables, it does not imply causation. Correlation does not equal causation.

blocks.title: Correlation vs. Causation
blocks.text: Just because two variables are correlated does not mean one causes the other. External factors or coincidences may drive the observed relationship.

points: Designing a fair experiment requires controlling variables to ensure unbiased results.
Linear regression models relationships between variables but does not imply causation.
Correlation between variables does not establish a causal link.
